eras.title: The Foundation & Nation-Building Era
eras.question: How do you turn independence into a republic?
eras.intro: Freedom arrived with Partition, violence and displacement. The new state had to integrate territory, protect citizenship and turn a constitutional promise into working institutions. Under Jawaharlal Nehru, elected government, economic planning and scientific investment became central to the national project. Yet these years also brought restrictions on rights, disputes over state autonomy and war.
eras.tension: The question was never only whether India could build institutions. It was how those institutions would use power: to protect individual rights, pursue social reform, accommodate regional demands and respond to insecurity.
events: Independence, and the trauma of Partition

British rule ended on 15 August 1947. The Independence Act created the independent Dominions of India and Pakistan. Partition brought mass displacement and communal violence alongside the transfer of power.

Independence and becoming a republic were different constitutional milestones. India began as a Dominion and became a republic in January 1950. For displaced families, the immediate concerns were safety, shelter, property and rebuilding livelihoods. Protecting minorities and rehabilitating refugees became urgent responsibilities of the new state.
Bringing the princely states into the Union
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon helped bring more than 500 princely states into India through accession and integration.
The process was not uniform. Junagadh, Hyderabad and Jammu and Kashmir followed different, contested paths. Territorial integration also continued beyond 1950.
War over Jammu and Kashmir follows Partition

Fighting over Jammu and Kashmir began in 1947. The dispute reached the UN Security Council in January 1948, and a ceasefire took effect on 1 January 1949. United Nations military observers arrived later that month.

Partition was followed almost immediately by armed conflict and competing territorial claims. The ceasefire stopped that phase of fighting without resolving the dispute. Its line and later arrangements should not be confused with a mutually agreed international boundary.
Nathuram Vinayak Godse assassinated Mahatma Gandhi at Birla House in Delhi on 30 January 1948, less than six months after independence.

The killing belongs within the history of the early republic, alongside constitution-making and state integration. Independence had not ended political violence or the struggle over communal coexistence.
An institutional base for atomic research

The Atomic Energy Commission was first established in August 1948 within the Department of Scientific Research. The Department of Atomic Energy followed on 3 August 1954 under the prime minister’s direct charge.

The commission and the department were different institutional steps. Their creation established a framework for research and administration, rather than demonstrating that India had already acquired nuclear weapons or a complete nuclear power industry.
The central bank enters public ownership
The Reserve Bank of India was nationalised with effect from 1 January 1949 under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948.

The RBI had begun operating in 1935, so public ownership did not mark its creation. Nor was this the same event as establishing SBI in 1955 or nationalising commercial banks in 1969. The central bank and a commercial bank have different functions.
Factory work receives a revised framework of protection
The Factories Act, 1948 came into force on 1 April 1949. It regulated covered factories through provisions on workers’ health, safety, welfare and working hours.

Industrial development concerned working conditions as well as output and investment. The Act’s scope did not encompass every worker in the economy. Statutory requirements, inspection and conditions inside workplaces need separate examination when assessing its effect.
A national museum opens before its permanent home
The National Museum was inaugurated at Rashtrapati Bhavan on 15 August 1949 by Governor-General C. Rajagopalachari. Its permanent building at Janpath was inaugurated on 18 December 1960.

The museum brought collections into a national public institution. Its opening and the move to a purpose-built home were separate milestones. Preserving objects, interpreting their histories and making collections accessible were continuing tasks rather than achievements completed on inauguration day.

The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. Most provisions came into force on 26 January 1950, when India became a republic. The Assembly’s drafting work had begun before independence, with B. R. Ambedkar chairing the Drafting Committee formed in August 1947.

The Constitution combined parliamentary government, fundamental rights, a federal distribution of powers and development goals in the Directive Principles. It was the product of an Assembly and its committees, not a document written by one person. Its original Preamble described a Sovereign Democratic Republic. The new framework soon faced disputes over the reach of rights and the powers needed for social reform.
The Election Commission of India was established on 25 January 1950, immediately before India became a republic. Its constitutional role provided the institutional basis for organising elections.

Universal adult franchise needed an administrative system as well as a constitutional promise. The Commission’s establishment in 1950 and the first general election in 1951–1952 were separate steps. Assessments of particular elections require their own evidence.
The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950, two days after the republic began. Its early sittings took place in part of the old Parliament House.

A Constitution needed institutions able to interpret and enforce it. The Court’s inauguration placed a new apex court within that framework. Disputes over rights, reform and the limits of government soon tested the relationship between elected institutions and the judiciary.
A Government of India resolution of 15 March 1950 established the Planning Commission. Its work concerned assessment of resources, development priorities and plans for their use.

The Commission was created by executive resolution, not as a constitutional body. Its establishment preceded the First Five-Year Plan. Planning was a method for coordinating public choices and investment in a country facing shortages of capital and infrastructure.
Planning begins with farms and irrigation

The First Five-Year Plan covered 1951–1956. It prioritised agriculture, irrigation and recovery in an economy still dealing with the disruption of Partition. Public planning aimed to allocate scarce resources towards development.

This was not a programme devoted mainly to heavy industry. The stronger emphasis on that objective came with the Second Plan. Reading the two plans separately makes the sequence clearer: stabilising and raising production in the early years, then placing greater weight on building industrial capacity.
Bhoodan seeks land redistribution through voluntary gifts
Vinoba Bhave’s visit to Pochampally on 18 April 1951 marked the beginning of the Bhoodan movement. It sought voluntary gifts of land for redistribution to landless people.

Bhoodan offered a route to land reform outside compulsory state acquisition. Promises of land, legally valid transfers and possession by recipients were different stages. Its place in rural politics should therefore be distinguished from a claim that landlessness was resolved.
The first amendment tests the new rights framework

The First Constitutional Amendment was enacted on 18 June 1951. It revised Article 19’s speech-restriction provisions, added Article 15(4), and introduced Articles 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule to protect specified reform legislation.

The amendment linked several debates: freedom of expression, measures for disadvantaged communities, state economic activity and land reform. The government’s stated justification followed court decisions. Its adoption demonstrates how early the tension between social reform and constitutional limits became a live political issue.
The first IIT is formally inaugurated

IIT Kharagpur was formally inaugurated by Education Minister Maulana Abul Kalam Azad on 18 August 1951. It became the first institute in the IIT system, following planning that began before independence.

Technical education formed part of the effort to build industrial and scientific capacity. The inauguration was one milestone in an institutional process, rather than the beginning of every kind of engineering education in India.
India held its first general election in 1951–1952. Congress won 364 of the 489 Lok Sabha seats with about 45% of the vote. Nehru continued as prime minister.

The roughly 74% seat share was much larger than the vote share, reflecting the first-past-the-post system. Congress’s dominance existed within a competitive election, not a legal one-party system. Voters initially qualified from age 21; organising rolls and voting across a largely non-literate electorate was a major administrative task.
Family planning enters national public-health policy

India launched a national family-planning programme in 1952, according to the National Health Mission’s historical account. It placed population and reproductive-health concerns within national health planning.

The programme’s existence in 1952 should be distinguished from the methods, targets and coercive practices associated with later periods. Access to services, informed choice and demographic change require different evidence. The date shown is a year-level milestone.
Community development creates an early rural programme
The Community Development Programme began on 2 October 1952, initially through selected development projects. Nehru inaugurated the programme at Alipur.

The programme placed rural development within an organised administrative effort before the Panchayati Raj experiments of the late 1950s. Government-led development projects and elected local self-government were different institutional arrangements. Their relationship helps explain the subsequent debate over participation in village development.
Music, dance and drama gain a national academy
President Rajendra Prasad inaugurated the Sangeet Natak Akademi on 28 January 1953 at Parliament House. It was established as a national institution for music, dance and drama.

Cultural institutions formed another part of nation-building alongside industry and universities. An academy offered an institutional setting for support and recognition. Its creation did not mark the beginning of the performing traditions themselves or establish equal support for every artist.
Andhra State precedes the wider linguistic reorganisation
Andhra State came into being on 1 October 1953 under the Andhra State Act. It was formed from specified territories of the existing Madras State.

This was an important step in the debate over language and state boundaries. Andhra State in 1953 and the larger Andhra Pradesh formed during the 1956 reorganisation were different arrangements. Reading them as a single event hides the sequence of change.
University funding and standards gain a national institution

The University Grants Commission was inaugurated on 28 December 1953. It became a statutory body in November 1956, with responsibilities for coordinating and maintaining standards in university education.

The institution’s beginnings and its statutory status were separate steps. Grants, standards, institutional autonomy and access to higher education raised different questions. The UGC’s creation complemented specialist institutions such as the IITs rather than marking the start of university education in India.
A national literary institution works across languages

The Sahitya Akademi was formally inaugurated on 12 March 1954 after a government resolution in December 1952. It was registered as a society on 7 January 1956 and functions as an autonomous organisation.

The new institution sought to support literature and exchange across Indian languages. The founding resolution, inauguration and society registration were distinct steps. Its multilingual remit adds another dimension to the language debates seen in state boundaries and government business.
Panchsheel sets out principles for coexistence
The five principles known as Panchsheel were formally stated in the preamble to the India–China agreement on trade and intercourse with the Tibet region of China, signed on 29 April 1954.

The principles included respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and peaceful coexistence. They expressed an approach to international relations. The 1962 war later exposed the distance between a diplomatic declaration and the security relationship it was intended to guide.
A civil route to marriage outside religious ceremony
The Special Marriage Act was enacted on 9 October 1954 and came into force on 1 January 1955. It provided a civil form of marriage, registration provisions and a framework for divorce.

The route allowed people of different religions to marry without one partner converting to the other’s religion, subject to statutory conditions and procedures. It stood alongside personal-law systems. Having a legal route and being able to use it safely were different parts of individual freedom.
From Bandung to a non-aligned movement

The 1955 Asian–African conference at Bandung brought newly independent countries and anti-colonial concerns into a wider diplomatic conversation. The first Non-Aligned Movement summit followed in Belgrade in 1961, with India among its founding participants.

Bandung and the formal establishment of the movement were separate milestones. Non-alignment sought room for independent judgment during the Cold War. It did not mean withdrawal from diplomacy or an absence of security interests.
A law against the practice of untouchability

Parliament enacted the Untouchability (Offences) Act in 1955 to punish practices prohibited by Article 17 of the Constitution. It was strengthened and renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976.

The constitutional ban came before this enforcement law. Neither should be confused with evidence that caste discrimination had ended. Later legislation addressed atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Marriage and divorce law is codified for covered communities
The Hindu Marriage Act was enacted on 18 May 1955. It codified conditions for marriage and provided for judicial separation and divorce for the people within its scope.

This was part of a series of reforms, followed by separate legislation on succession, adoption and maintenance. It was not a uniform marriage code for every Indian. The original provisions and changes made by later amendments need to be read separately.
The State Bank of India is created
On 1 July 1955, the Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India, a state-owned institution.

Public ownership in Indian banking did not begin with the nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969. SBI was an earlier institutional step. Ownership, branch reach and actual access to useful financial services remain different questions.
Citizenship gets a continuing statutory framework

The Citizenship Act was enacted on 30 December 1955. It provided for acquisition and termination of Indian citizenship through a statutory framework following the Constitution’s provisions on citizenship at its commencement.

Birth, descent, registration and naturalisation were distinct routes governed by legal conditions. Later amendments changed the framework. Today’s eligibility rules should not be projected backwards onto the law as originally enacted in 1955.
The Second Plan puts heavy industry at the centre

The Second Five-Year Plan, covering 1956–1961, placed greater emphasis on industrialisation, capital formation and heavy industry, while also addressing agriculture, transport, power and smaller enterprises.

The strategy sought to build productive capacity over time. It was not simply the First Plan continued under a new name. The shift helps explain why steel, machinery, technical education and large public investments occupy such a prominent place in accounts of the Nehru years.
AIIMS combines medical teaching, research and care

AIIMS in New Delhi was created in 1956 through an Act of Parliament as an autonomous institution of national importance. Its mandate linked medical education and training with research and health care.

A specialist teaching institution and a nationwide system of accessible primary care perform different roles. AIIMS’s establishment should be read alongside later efforts to strengthen rural health services, rather than as a substitute for them.
Inheritance law changes, with inequalities still remaining
The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 codified inheritance rules for the people to whom it applied. Daughters were included among Class I heirs, and the Act addressed women’s property rights.

The 1956 framework did not give daughters the same position as sons in Mitakshara coparcenary property. That distinction matters when reading the 2005 amendment. These were changes within a particular succession-law framework, not a single inheritance code for every Indian.
Oil exploration gains a dedicated public commission

The Oil and Natural Gas Directorate was converted into the Oil and Natural Gas Commission on 14 August 1956. This followed the creation of an oil and gas division within the Geological Survey of India in 1955.

The change gave petroleum exploration a stronger public institutional base during the Second Plan period. The commission of 1956 should be distinguished from the later corporate form of ONGC. Creating an exploration organisation did not itself establish oil self-sufficiency.
Life insurance is consolidated in a public corporation
The Life Insurance Corporation of India came into existence on 1 September 1956 following nationalisation of the life-insurance business. LIC was established under its own Act of Parliament.

This was a different institutional change from creating SBI or nationalising commercial banks. Its stated purpose included extending life insurance, particularly in rural areas. Public ownership, wider sales and adequate protection for households remained separate measures.
B. R. Ambedkar embraced Buddhism at Nagpur on 14 October 1956. The event became a major milestone in his life and in the history of the Buddhist conversion movement in India.

The chapter’s social history extends beyond legislation passed by the state. Religious choice and collective identity were also part of struggles over dignity and caste. Ambedkar’s conversion belongs alongside his constitutional work, without reducing either to the other.
The States Reorganisation Act reorganised state boundaries substantially along linguistic lines. Demands for language-based states had already produced Andhra State in 1953.
Reorganisation accommodated regional identities within the Union. It did not settle every boundary dispute, and further states were created in later decades.
The rupee moves to a decimal system

Decimal coinage took effect on 1 April 1957. The rupee was divided into 100 paise in place of the earlier system of 16 annas or 64 pice. The new unit was called naya paisa to distinguish it during the transition.

The change reached everyday pricing, accounting and cash transactions. It altered the rupee’s subdivisions rather than creating a new national currency. The transition required people and institutions to work between familiar denominations and the new decimal units.
An elected Communist government, then dismissal
E. M. S. Namboodiripad’s ministry took office in Kerala on 5 April 1957 after an election. In 1959, the Congress-led Union government dismissed it under Article 356; its tenure ended on 31 July.

The episode reveals both electoral competition beneath Congress’s national dominance and an early dispute over federal power. The election and the dismissal belong in the same account. NCERT describes the dismissal as a controversial use of constitutional emergency powers.
New public-sector plants begin producing hot metal

Rourkela Steel Plant produced its first hot metal on 3 February 1959. Bhilai followed on 4 February. These were major steps in the public-sector steel programme associated with the Second Five-Year Plan.

Hot-metal production was a stage in commissioning integrated plants, rather than evidence that every steelmaking and rolling unit was complete. India already had a private steel industry. The new plants expanded the public sector’s role in building industrial capacity.
Television begins as a limited public-service experiment
Public-service television broadcasting began experimentally on 15 September 1959. Prasar Bharati traces Doordarshan’s beginnings to this small-scale experiment within All India Radio.

The experimental start was distinct from later regular service and nationwide expansion. Television’s eventual reach should not be projected back onto 1959. The milestone adds broadcasting and communication to the era’s account of new public institutions.
An early Panchayati Raj experiment begins in Rajasthan
Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959. The initiative formed part of the early post-independence effort to develop local self-government.

Local institutions and village councils had earlier histories. The 1959 milestone also preceded the 73rd Constitutional Amendment by decades. State-led arrangements, elected participation and the actual transfer of functions and resources were different stages of decentralisation.
Bombay State is divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat
The Bombay Reorganisation Act was enacted on 25 April 1960. Maharashtra and Gujarat came into existence on 1 May, dividing the bilingual Bombay State.

The 1956 reorganisation had not settled every demand for language-based states. The 1960 change extended that process. A shared linguistic identity could support a demand for statehood without removing disagreements over territory, resources or political representation.
India and Pakistan sign the Indus Waters Treaty
India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty on 19 September 1960 after years of negotiations facilitated by the World Bank. It established a framework for using the waters of the Indus basin.

Partition had divided a connected river and irrigation system across two countries. The treaty showed negotiated cooperation on a technical and economic issue despite wider political disputes. This entry describes the 1960 agreement, without treating its later history as part of the signing itself.
Parliament prohibits dowry through a national law
The Dowry Prohibition Act was enacted on 20 May 1961 and came into force on 1 July. It provided penalties for giving, taking and demanding dowry, subject to the Act’s definitions and terms.

The law’s existence did not establish that the practice had ended. Its original design, subsequent amendments and the separate development of criminal-law protections require attention to their dates. Social pressure and access to enforcement shaped what a prohibition meant in practice.
Indian military action ended Portuguese rule in Goa, Daman and Diu in December 1961. Goa commemorates its liberation on 19 December.
The end of British rule in 1947 had not ended every colonial presence in the subcontinent. Goa was initially administered within a Union Territory and attained statehood in 1987.
War with China tests the early vision
The Sino-Indian War exposed serious weaknesses in India's defence preparedness and strained the assumptions behind relations with China.
The conflict pushed defence and border security higher on the national agenda. Non-alignment did not remove the need for military capability.
Parliament provides for continuing the use of English

The Official Languages Act was enacted on 10 May 1963. It provided for the continued use of English, alongside Hindi, for specified Union official purposes and parliamentary business after the Constitution’s initial fifteen-year transition.

The issue concerned the working languages of government and Parliament. It did not designate one language as the language of every Indian. The 1963 law and later amendments belonged to an ongoing negotiation over language, access and the federal balance.
Bhakra Dam is dedicated after years of construction
Nehru dedicated Bhakra Dam to the nation on 22 October 1963. The wider Bhakra–Nangal project combined irrigation and power generation, with some benefits beginning before the main dam’s completion.

The project connected agricultural development with investment in electricity and infrastructure. A dedication date was not the start of every benefit or the end of every related work. Assessing a large project also meant examining the distribution of water, power, costs and impacts on affected communities.
A sounding rocket launches from Thumba
A Nike-Apache sounding rocket, procured from the United States, launched from Thumba on 21 November 1963. The programme supported scientific investigation of the upper atmosphere.

A sounding rocket collects measurements on a suborbital flight; it does not place a satellite in orbit. The launch preceded ISRO’s formation in 1969. These distinctions help separate the beginnings of space research from later satellite and launch-vehicle milestones.
Nagaland becomes a state within the Union
Nagaland came into existence as a state on 1 December 1963. Statehood created a new political and administrative arrangement within the Indian Union.

The transition followed a regional movement and negotiations. It should not be read as the end of every conflict over Naga identity or political aspirations. The northeastern story involved different movements and constitutional arrangements, rather than a single uniform process of integration.
Nehru’s death closes the first premiership
Jawaharlal Nehru died on 27 May 1964, ending the premiership he had held since independence in August 1947.

His death provides a useful boundary for this chapter, not a claim that every institution or policy changed at once. India entered its next leadership transition with constitutional government established, major development programmes under way and unresolved questions over security, inequality and regional demands.
overview: Begin with independence and the republic as separate milestones. Partition left urgent questions about territory, citizenship and rebuilding lives. Accession, the Constitution and the 1955 Citizenship Act addressed different parts of the new state. The resulting legal framework also faced early tests over speech, social reform and federal power.

Follow development through institutions, projects and daily life. The First and Second Plans placed different weights on agriculture and heavy industry. Factory protections addressed working conditions; community development and Bhoodan took different approaches to rural change. SBI, LIC, the UGC and the IITs served distinct purposes. Steel plants and Bhakra show construction becoming operational, while decimal coinage and experimental television changed other parts of everyday infrastructure. Oil exploration gained a dedicated commission, while the National Museum and the academies for performing arts and literature placed cultural work within new national institutions.

Read social reform and regional accommodation alongside national institutions. Civil marriage, Hindu-law reform and laws against untouchability and dowry addressed different inequalities. Family planning entered public-health policy, while Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion placed dignity and religious choice within the wider social story. Panchayati Raj, state reorganisation, official languages and Nagaland show several ways power and identity were negotiated. Relations with Pakistan and China followed contrasting paths through treaty and war.

eras.title: Wars, Food Security & Social Transition
eras.question: What does security mean when food is scarce?
eras.intro: After Nehru’s death, leadership passed first to Shastri and then to Indira Gandhi. War, drought and food shortages tested the state. New agricultural methods, dairy cooperatives and public banking changed development policy, while Congress lost ground, split and rebuilt its mandate. By 1975, economic pressure, protests and a contested election had brought government and opposition into open confrontation.
eras.tension: Security had several meanings in these years: defending borders, securing food, finding work and protecting political rights. Measures intended to strengthen the state also raised questions about who controlled its institutions and who benefited from its policies.
events: Shastri succeeds Nehru after an interim premiership
Lal Bahadur Shastri became prime minister on 9 June 1964. Gulzari Lal Nanda had served as interim prime minister following Nehru’s death on 27 May.

The succession matters in its own right: constitutional government continued after the death of the leader who had dominated the first years of independence. Shastri’s short premiership would face war with Pakistan and severe pressure on food supplies.
A public institution for grain procurement and distribution

The Food Corporation of India was established in 1965 under the Food Corporations Act, 1964, against a background of grain shortages. Its functions included price-support operations, grain movement and stocks for food security.

Food security depended on more than higher-yielding seeds. Procurement, storage, transport and distribution connected farm output with public policy. FCI’s creation should be distinguished from the later 2013 statutory framework for household entitlements.
A national institution takes shape around dairy cooperatives
The National Dairy Development Board was founded in 1965 at Anand. Its approach placed milk producers and the professionals employed by their cooperatives at the centre of dairy development.

The board supplied an institutional foundation before Operation Flood began in 1970. Cooperative ownership, technical support and reliable marketing were distinct parts of the dairy strategy; higher production alone does not describe it.
Agricultural pricing gains a dedicated advisory institution
The Agricultural Prices Commission came into existence in January 1965. It was renamed the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices in 1985. Its role was to advise on agricultural support prices.

Price advice, government price decisions and actual procurement are different steps. The commission belongs alongside the Food Corporation of India in the account of food security, but the two institutions performed different functions. A recommended price did not establish that every farmer sold at that price.
War and the call for food security
India and Pakistan fought their second war in 1965. Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri's Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan linked the soldier and the farmer.
Military security and food supply became closely connected national priorities. The Tashkent agreement followed in January 1966.

The Green Revolution grew from trials of improved varieties and a wider package of irrigation, fertiliser, agronomic practices and public support. ICAR’s account records wheat trials and demonstrations in the early to mid-1960s. M. S. Swaminathan and Norman Borlaug were key scientific contributors.

It was not a single seed launch or a transformation shared equally by every farm. Access to water, credit and markets shaped the gains. Procurement and storage institutions mattered alongside research. Higher national grain output also did not automatically mean that every household had adequate nutrition.
Tashkent seeks to restore relations after the war

Shastri and Pakistan’s President Ayub Khan signed the Tashkent Declaration on 10 January 1966. It provided for withdrawal to positions held before 5 August 1965 and steps towards restoring normal relations.

The declaration addressed the aftermath of the 1965 war without resolving every underlying dispute. Shastri died in Tashkent on 11 January, creating another leadership transition immediately after the diplomatic agreement.
Indira Gandhi took office on 24 January 1966 after Shastri’s death and a second interim premiership by Nanda.

The leadership change occurred within Congress rule, but it did not mean the party’s internal balance of power remained settled. Her relationship with senior party leaders would become a major conflict later in the decade.
Annual Plans interrupt the five-year sequence
Three Annual Plans covered 1966–1969 between the Third and Fourth Five-Year Plans.

The familiar list of Five-Year Plans can hide this interval. Annual planning did not mean that public planning disappeared. Reading the sequence alongside food shortages, foreign-exchange constraints and the 1966 devaluation gives a fuller account of the pressure on economic policy.
On 6 June 1966, India devalued the rupee. RBI’s chronology records a 36.5% reduction in its external value.

A fall in the currency’s value and the corresponding rise in the rupee price of a foreign currency are different percentage calculations. The decision belongs in the history of India’s external-payments difficulties, rather than being confused with the later 1991 reforms.
Punjab is reorganised; Haryana becomes a state

The Punjab Reorganisation Act took effect on 1 November 1966. It created Haryana, reorganised Punjab, established Chandigarh as a Union Territory and transferred specified hill areas to Himachal Pradesh.

Linguistic reorganisation continued after the major settlement of 1956. Boundaries also required arrangements for shared institutions and resources, making the practical terms of federalism as important as the new map.
Congress loses ground in the states

Congress retained power at the Centre in the 1967 elections but suffered major setbacks in state assemblies. The DMK won power in Madras state, while non-Congress coalitions formed in several other states.

The results brought regional parties and opposition cooperation into government well before the national coalition era of the 1990s. Single-party regional success and multi-party coalitions were different routes away from Congress dominance.
National education policy develops across decades
The National Policy on Education of 1968 set out a framework for educational development. A new policy followed in 1986 and was modified in 1992.

Education policy therefore had a long history before NEP 2020. A policy document, a constitutional right and an enforceable statutory entitlement are different instruments. The later Right to Education framework should not be treated as another name for these earlier policies.
Language policy adds safeguards for the continued use of English

The Official Languages (Amendment) Act, 1967 received presidential assent on 8 January 1968. It strengthened the framework for continuing English alongside Hindi for Union official purposes. Section 3(5) required resolutions from all state legislatures that had not adopted Hindi as their official language, followed by resolutions in both Houses of Parliament, before specified uses of English could be discontinued.

The settlement concerned official administration, not the declaration of a national language. Its consent requirements show how language diversity shaped the rules of the Union. The year in the Act’s title differs from the date of presidential assent.

Indira Gandhi’s government nationalised 14 major commercial banks with effect from 19 July 1969. The Banking Companies Act of 1970 subsequently provided a framework with retrospective commencement tied to that date.

The policy sought to use banking for wider development goals, including rural credit and access. It followed earlier public ownership of the RBI and the creation of SBI. A change of ownership was a concrete institutional step; the reach and quality of lending require separate evidence.
The Indian Space Research Organisation was formed on 15 August 1969, succeeding INCOSPAR, which had been established in 1962.
Later lunar and planetary missions grew from institutions built over decades. Early ambitions included applying space technology to development, rather than concentrating only on exploration.
Conflict between Indira Gandhi and the Congress organisation’s senior leadership culminated in a party split in 1969. Rival groups became known as Congress (R) and Congress (O).
The dispute involved leadership, policy and control of the party. Congress dominance after independence therefore cannot be treated as one continuous, internally unified political arrangement.
NDDB launched Operation Flood in 1970 under Verghese Kurien’s leadership. The programme developed cooperative links between milk producers and urban consumers and continued in phases through 1996.

The dairy transformation had different institutions and techniques from the grain-focused Green Revolution. Producer organisation, procurement and marketing were central. Calling both a revolution should not hide those differences or imply that their later outcomes had all been achieved in 1970.
Contract labour receives a framework for regulation and selective abolition

The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act was enacted on 5 September 1970 and came into force on 10 February 1971. It provided for establishment registration, contractor licensing, welfare duties and government prohibition of contract labour in specified work after consultation.

The law did not abolish every form of contract labour. It linked regulation of employment conditions to a procedure for prohibition, making implementation and enforcement central to its effect on workers.
Himachal Pradesh becomes a full state
Himachal Pradesh attained full statehood on 25 January 1971. Its territory had expanded in 1966 when hill areas were transferred from Punjab.

The sequence distinguishes a change in territorial boundaries from a change in constitutional status. The creation of a state brought a different place within the federal system, alongside the continuing challenges of governing a mountainous region.
A renewed mandate built around Garibi Hatao
Indira Gandhi’s Congress campaigned on Garibi Hatao and won a decisive majority in the 1971 Lok Sabha election.
The victory followed the party split and restored her parliamentary strength. An electoral mandate and the eventual effects of anti-poverty policies are different questions.
India and the Soviet Union sign a twenty-year treaty

India and the Soviet Union signed the Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation in New Delhi on 9 August 1971. Its provisions covered consultation, cooperation and relations between the two countries.

The treaty preceded the December war and was an important part of India’s diplomatic position during the East Pakistan crisis. It should be read alongside the earlier claim to independent foreign-policy judgment, rather than treating non-alignment as an absence of strategic relationships.
War and the creation of Bangladesh
The liberation struggle in East Pakistan, repression and a major refugee influx preceded the December India–Pakistan war. Pakistan's forces in the east surrendered on 16 December.
Bangladesh emerged as an independent country. Its liberation involved Bangladeshi resistance and Indian military intervention, rather than a war fought by India alone.
Privy purses and official recognition of rulers end
The 26th Constitutional Amendment received assent on 28 December 1971. It ended constitutional recognition of the former princely rulers and abolished privy purses through Article 363A.

These arrangements had formed part of the settlement around the integration of princely states. Their abolition was a later constitutional change. It should not be described as the moment when the princely states first joined India.
New states and Union Territories reshape the Northeast

The North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 took effect on 21 January 1972. Manipur and Tripura became states, Meghalaya became a state, and Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became Union Territories.

These were different constitutional arrangements, not five simultaneous grants of statehood. The changes widened the range of federal institutions available to address regional aspirations; they did not by themselves resolve every conflict over identity, representation or autonomy.
A new patent framework takes effect
Most provisions of the Patents Act, 1970 came into force on 20 April 1972 with the publication of the Patent Rules, 1972, according to the patent office’s historical account.

The milestone concerned the legal framework for inventions, not the announcement of a particular technology. The original Act and its later amendments need to be read separately. Rules on protection, licensing and access formed another part of industrial policy alongside public ownership and production planning.
Coal nationalisation extends public ownership into energy supply

Coal nationalisation proceeded in stages. Most coking coal mines were nationalised on 1 May 1972, with specified steel-company exceptions; the nationalisation of non-coking coal mines followed on 1 May 1973.

Alongside bank nationalisation, the coal measures expanded state ownership in a sector essential to industry and electricity. Changes of ownership should be distinguished from later assessments of production, safety, investment and labour conditions.
The Simla Agreement follows the war

India and Pakistan signed the Simla Agreement on 2 July 1972. They committed to peaceful settlement through bilateral negotiations or other mutually agreed means and to respecting the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir.
The agreement followed the 1971 war. It established a diplomatic framework but did not settle the Kashmir dispute or convert the Line of Control into an agreed international border.
A national framework for wildlife protection
The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 created a legal framework covering wildlife protection, regulated hunting and protected areas.

The legislation and the practical work of protecting habitats are separate parts of conservation. Later amendments changed the framework. This entry describes its 1972 origins rather than treating today’s amended law as identical to the original.
Gratuity receives a statutory payment framework
The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 came into force on 16 September 1972. It established a framework for gratuity payments to employees in covered establishments, subject to the Act’s conditions.

The law addressed an employment benefit distinct from wages or a pension. Coverage and eligibility mattered, so the statute should not be read as a universal retirement payment for every worker. Its practical effect depended on compliance and access to remedies.
General insurance moves into public ownership

The General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 nationalised general insurance with effect from 1 January 1973. IRDAI’s historical account records the amalgamation of 107 insurers into four companies.

This was separate from the nationalisation of life insurance in 1956 and major banks in 1969. The sequence shows public ownership expanding across different financial services. Consolidating ownership did not by itself settle questions of coverage, service or claims handling.
Chipko brings local forest protection into public view
Chipko protests emerged in the Chamoli region in 1973. The 1974 action at Reni became a prominent episode in which village women resisted tree felling.

Forest protection involved the people who depended on forests as well as government conservation programmes. Chipko therefore belongs alongside the Wildlife Protection Act and Project Tiger while representing a different form of action. Its local episodes should not be collapsed into one demonstration or one leader’s work.
Project Tiger launched in April 1973 to conserve tigers and their habitats. It became a major national conservation programme.

A species-focused programme and a broader wildlife law are different instruments. Evaluating results requires evidence on populations, habitat connectivity, management and the experiences of communities living near protected areas. A programme’s launch does not itself establish those outcomes.
Limits on the power to amend
On 24 April 1973, the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament’s constitutional amendment power did not extend to destroying the Constitution’s basic structure.

The decision addressed the limits of constitutional change, not a general prohibition on amendment. It emerged from disputes over rights, property and reform and became a central reference point in later institutional confrontations. It helps connect the policy arguments of this era with the constitutional crisis that followed.
The oil shock adds to domestic economic strain
The 1973 international oil-price shock added inflationary pressure to an economy already affected by war and drought. RBI’s historical account identifies several such pressures during this period.

Higher import costs fed into wider economic difficulties. Public anger over prices and shortages had more than one cause, so it should not be explained entirely by either a global shock or a single domestic decision.
Student protests become a wider political challenge

Student-led protests in Gujarat and Bihar in 1974 challenged price rises, corruption and government conduct. Jayaprakash Narayan became a central leader of the Bihar movement and called for Total Revolution.

The movements widened the challenge to Congress rule. Protest, opposition-party strategy and constitutional government became increasingly entangled. Their development helps explain the political confrontation before the Emergency, without making its declaration inevitable.
Water-pollution control gains a statutory board system

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted on 23 March 1974. It provided for pollution-control boards and measures to prevent and control water pollution. The Central Pollution Control Board was constituted in September 1974 under the Act.

The Act’s passage and the establishment of its central institution were separate milestones. A regulatory framework did not establish clean water everywhere. Monitoring, consent procedures and enforcement became practical responsibilities alongside the expansion of industry and urban settlements.
A nationwide railway strike confronts the government
Railway workers struck in May 1974 over pay and working conditions, with George Fernandes prominent in the leadership. The government opposed the strike and arrested union leaders.

The dispute brought labour rights and the operation of an essential national network into conflict. The ILO record and contemporary union and management papers preserve competing accounts. Those perspectives should be identified rather than treating every participant’s allegation as an established finding.
The first nuclear test at Pokhran
India conducted its first underground nuclear test on 18 May 1974, commonly called Smiling Buddha. The government described it as a peaceful nuclear explosion.
It demonstrated nuclear explosive capability. The 1998 tests were a later milestone in India's declared nuclear posture.
India wins the men’s hockey World Cup
India defeated Pakistan 2–1 in the men’s hockey World Cup final at Kuala Lumpur on 15 March 1975.

The victory adds sport to a period often described through wars and political crises. It also places hockey’s international achievements before the cricket World Cup victory of 1983, keeping the two sports’ histories distinct.
Aryabhata, India’s first satellite, launched on 19 April 1975. It was designed and fabricated in India and carried into orbit by a Soviet Kosmos-3M rocket from Kapustin Yar.

Building a satellite and independently launching one are different technical achievements. Aryabhata demonstrated Indian spacecraft development while relying on international launch cooperation. That distinction matters when tracing the later space programme.
Sikkim became India’s 22nd state on 16 May 1975 through the constitutional transition associated with the 36th Amendment.

This was a later change in the Union, distinct from the accession and integration of princely states around independence. Statehood also requires attention to the region’s own political history, rather than treating the national map as fixed in 1947.
The election case reaches a constitutional crisis

On 12 June 1975, the Allahabad High Court set aside Indira Gandhi’s 1971 election from Rae Bareli. On 24 June, the Supreme Court granted a conditional stay, allowing her to continue as prime minister while restricting her participation as a member of Parliament.

The High Court ruling, the interim Supreme Court order and the subsequent Emergency were distinct events. The conditional stay did not finally decide the appeal. This chapter ends at that confrontation; the declaration of Emergency is covered in the next era.
overview: Start with the succession after Nehru. The two leadership changes were constitutional transitions, but they occurred amid military and economic pressure. The war and the Tashkent agreement belong alongside the food crisis, not in a separate story with no domestic consequences.

Follow the institutions behind development. Agricultural price advice, grain procurement, dairy cooperatives, bank ownership and general insurance served different purposes. Coal nationalisation and patent reform addressed different parts of industrial policy. Contract-labour and gratuity laws added employment protections. The dates of decisions matter, but each also needs examination through coverage and implementation.

Read political competition, regional change and social action together. New states, language safeguards and opposition victories changed federal politics. Wildlife protection, Chipko and water-pollution regulation took different approaches to environmental concerns, while hockey supplied a major sporting milestone. The Congress split, its renewed mandate, economic strain and protest lead to the court orders of June 1975. The Emergency begins the next chapter.

eras.title: Political Turmoil & the Coalition Turn
eras.question: How resilient are democratic institutions?
eras.intro: The Emergency restricted political freedom. Voters removed the government in 1977, but the alternative soon fractured. The following decade combined new technology and education programmes with regional conflict, targeted violence and a struggle over representation. By 1991, national power depended increasingly on alliances and outside support.
eras.tension: Elections restored competition after the Emergency. They did not settle questions about executive power, minority security or social representation. The contrast between negotiated peace in Mizoram and escalating violence elsewhere shows why each regional conflict needs its own history.
events: A national Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 under Indira Gandhi. Opposition leaders were detained and the press faced censorship.
Coercive sterilisation and demolitions became enduring symbols of abuse. This internal Emergency must be distinguished from earlier emergencies declared over external threats.
Child development services begin through local projects

The Integrated Child Development Services scheme launched on 2 October 1975, initially through 33 projects across India. It addressed the nutrition, health and development needs of young children and support for mothers.

The scheme linked several services rather than offering only a food transfer. Its initial projects should be distinguished from later expansion through Anganwadi services. Programme coverage, staffing, service quality and children’s nutritional outcomes require separate evidence.
Abolition targets bonded labour and bonded debt

An ordinance abolished the bonded labour system in October 1975. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, enacted on 9 February 1976, was deemed effective from 25 October 1975. It freed bonded labourers from service obligations and extinguished liability to repay bonded debt.

Legal abolition did not establish the disappearance of coercive labour. Identification, release and rehabilitation remained separate responsibilities. The reform belongs in the Emergency period alongside scrutiny of the government’s restrictions on civil liberties.
Equal remuneration becomes a statutory obligation

The Equal Remuneration Act was enacted on 11 February 1976. It required equal remuneration for men and women performing the same work or work of a similar nature, and addressed discrimination in recruitment.

The legal test concerned comparable work, not an automatic guarantee of equal earnings across the economy. Occupational segregation, access to employment and enforcement therefore remain distinct questions when assessing women’s economic position.

Enacted during the Emergency, the 42nd Amendment added Socialist and Secular to the Preamble, introduced Fundamental Duties and inserted environmental provisions, alongside wider institutional changes.

Its changes included attempts to restrict judicial review. The amendment belongs within the history of concentrated executive power as well as social and environmental provisions. Read it alongside the post-Emergency constitutional changes, including the 44th Amendment.
The Janata Party won the general election, and Morarji Desai led the first non-Congress government at the Union level.
The result demonstrated the force of electoral accountability. Internal divisions later weakened Janata, and Congress returned to power in 1980.
The Janata government appointed the Shah Commission in 1977 to investigate abuses committed during the Emergency.
Its inquiry examined the use of administrative and police power. Documenting abuses and securing accountability were separate tasks.

The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978 received assent on 30 April 1979. It replaced internal disturbance with armed rebellion as a ground for an internal Emergency and required written Cabinet advice.

It protected enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 from suspension through Article 359 and strengthened parliamentary checks on emergency powers. Different provisions commenced on different dates. The Act’s 1978 title is not its assent date.
Janata fractures and Charan Singh takes office
The Janata government lost its majority. Charan Singh became prime minister on 28 July 1979, initially relying on Congress support.
That support was withdrawn. His short premiership and caretaker period led into the January 1980 election.
Indira Gandhi’s Congress won the January 1980 general election, returning her to the prime minister’s office.
The result followed the fragmentation of Janata. The electoral rejection of the Emergency in 1977 had not created a durable governing alternative.
An Indian launch vehicle places Rohini in orbit
On 18 July 1980, SLV-3 launched the Rohini RS-1 satellite from Sriharikota. It marked India’s first successful satellite launch using its own launch vehicle.
India had already built satellites launched on foreign rockets. The new capability concerned the launch vehicle as well as the satellite, and followed the first experimental SLV-3 flight in 1979.
Forest diversion becomes subject to central approval

The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 was deemed to come into force on 25 October 1980. It required prior Central Government approval for state decisions such as dereservation of reserved forests and use of forest land for non-forest purposes.

This added a national approval requirement to decisions over forest land. It was a different legal instrument from wildlife protection or pollution control. Approval procedures and the ecological consequences of individual projects require separate examination.
Air-pollution control gains a dedicated statute

The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 came into force on 16 May 1981. It provided a legal framework for preventing, controlling and reducing air pollution, with responsibilities assigned to pollution-control boards.

The Act extended the regulatory story beyond the Water Act of 1974. A statutory framework did not establish cleaner air everywhere. Monitoring, industrial controls and enforcement remained practical tests alongside the growth of cities and industry.
NABARD takes on rural development finance
NABARD came into existence on 12 July 1982, taking over agricultural credit functions from the RBI and refinance functions from the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation.

The institution formed part of a longer effort to finance agriculture and rural development. It should not be confused with a retail bank opening an account for every farmer or with a direct cash-transfer scheme.
New Delhi hosts the ninth Asian Games
The ninth Asian Games took place in New Delhi from 19 November to 4 December 1982. India hosted athletes from across Asia in a multi-sport event.

Hosting belongs in the period’s sporting history alongside the 1983 cricket World Cup victory, but it was a different kind of achievement. Event organisation, infrastructure and athlete performance need distinct assessment. The Games also placed Delhi at the centre of a major international gathering.
India wins its first cricket World Cup
Kapil Dev's team defeated the West Indies at Lord's on 25 June 1983 to win India's first men's Cricket World Cup.
The victory became a lasting sporting landmark. It should not be treated as the sole cause of cricket's later commercial and broadcasting expansion.
INSAT-1B connects space capability to everyday communications

INSAT-1B launched on 30 August 1983 and reached full operational capability in October after difficulties deploying its solar array. The satellite provided communication circuits and returned Earth imagery.

The mission adds a service dimension to the story of launch vehicles and research institutions. Launch, successful deployment and routine operation were separate achievements. Space infrastructure became part of communications and observation systems used on the ground.
Rakesh Sharma flies to space aboard Soyuz T-11
Indian Air Force pilot Rakesh Sharma launched aboard Soyuz T-11 on 3 April 1984 as part of the Soviet Interkosmos programme, becoming the first Indian citizen in space.

The flight was an achievement through international cooperation. It was distinct from launching a person aboard an Indian-built spacecraft or launch vehicle. Crewed flight, satellite services and domestic launch capability developed through different programmes and milestones.
The Army entered the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar during Operation Blue Star, targeting armed militants.
The operation caused casualties and damage to the Akal Takht and deepened a traumatic conflict. Religious significance and civilian experiences are essential to understanding its impact.
The Centre for Development of Telematics was established in August 1984 to develop Indian telecom technology.
Its work on digital switching and rural exchanges formed part of a longer technology story. Telecom expansion preceded smartphones, UPI and the Digital India programme.
Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October by two Sikh bodyguards. Anti-Sikh killings followed in Delhi and other places.
Describing these events only as riots obscures targeted violence against Sikhs. Accountability and justice remained major public issues long afterwards.
Bhopal exposes the human cost of industrial failure
A release of methyl isocyanate from the Union Carbide India pesticide plant during the night of 2–3 December caused mass deaths and injuries in Bhopal.

The disaster raises questions about industrial safety, emergency preparedness and corporate accountability. Death estimates differ by source and time period. A single number should not be presented without explaining what it counts.
The 52nd Constitutional Amendment introduced the Tenth Schedule in 1985, providing for disqualification on specified grounds of political defection by legislators.

The framework sought to address party-switching, but also raised questions about party discipline and legislators’ independence. Its original text and later amendments must be distinguished. A change in party affiliation and a legally determined disqualification are not automatically the same event.
The Assam Accord addresses a regional movement
The Union and Assam governments signed the Assam Accord on 15 August with the All Assam Students’ Union and All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad after years of agitation.

The agreement addressed migration, safeguards for Assamese identity and economic development. Its text differentiated arrivals before 1966, during 1966–1971 and on or after 25 March 1971. Signing the Accord and implementing its provisions were separate processes.
India joins its neighbours in founding SAARC
The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation was established with the signing of its Charter in Dhaka on 8 December 1985. India was one of its seven founding members.

A standing regional forum created another channel for cooperation alongside bilateral diplomacy. Its establishment should be distinguished from later results in trade, connectivity or dispute resolution. The chapter’s security conflicts did not exhaust India’s relationships with its neighbours.
Education policy moves towards school improvements
The 1986 National Policy on Education set out a new national framework. Operation Blackboard followed in 1987–1988 to improve facilities in primary schools.

The scheme provided for classrooms, teachers and teaching materials. A policy commitment, a funded scheme and conditions inside a classroom are different measures of progress. The policy was modified in 1992.
Environmental protection gains an umbrella law
The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted on 23 May 1986. It provided a broad framework for Union government action to protect and improve the environment.

It followed earlier legislation on specific environmental subjects and the 1984 Bhopal disaster. The chronological connection should not be reduced to a claim that one event alone produced the law. Enforcement, monitoring and remedies require their own assessment.
The Mizoram Accord creates a route to peace

The Mizoram Memorandum of Settlement was signed on 30 June 1986 by MNF leader Laldenga, Union Home Secretary R. D. Pradhan and Mizoram Chief Secretary Lalkhama. It followed years of insurgency and negotiations.

The settlement offered a constitutional and political route out of armed conflict. It should be studied on its own terms, alongside other regional agreements. Different movements had different demands, histories and outcomes.
Consumer disputes gain a dedicated legal framework

The Consumer Protection Act was enacted on 24 December 1986, with provisions commencing in 1987. It provided for a three-tier system for consumer dispute redressal at district, state and national levels.

The law gave consumer complaints a specialised institutional route. Passing the Act and establishing functioning forums were different steps. Access, delay and enforcement matter when assessing whether the promised remedies reached consumers.
Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh become states
The Union Territories of Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became states on 20 February 1987. The date marked a change in their constitutional status within the Union.

Mizoram’s statehood followed the 1986 accord, while Arunachal Pradesh had a different political and administrative history. Sharing a statehood date does not make their routes identical. These changes also differed from the Union Territory arrangements introduced in 1972.
Bofors allegations bring defence procurement under scrutiny

A Swedish Radio broadcast on 16 April 1987 alleged payoffs linked to India’s Bofors gun contract. The controversy reached the Lok Sabha, where a statement on the purchase was made on 20 April. The Supreme Court later recounted the allegations’ emergence in Union of India v. W. N. Chadha.

This milestone records the allegations and the public accountability dispute, not a finding of individual guilt. Procurement decisions, reported payments, investigations and later judicial outcomes are distinct parts of the case. The controversy formed part of the political pressures of the late 1980s.
Goa becomes a state while Daman and Diu remain a Union Territory
Goa attained statehood on 30 May 1987 when the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu was reorganised. Daman and Diu continued together as a Union Territory.

The event came more than twenty-five years after Portuguese rule ended in 1961. Territorial incorporation and statehood were separate milestones, showing how an area’s constitutional position within India changed over time.
The Indo-Lanka Accord and military intervention
Rajiv Gandhi and President J. R. Jayewardene signed the Indo-Lanka Accord on 29 July 1987. India deployed the Indian Peace Keeping Force in Sri Lanka.
The deployment developed into armed conflict with the LTTE. Indian forces withdrew in 1990. The agreement’s diplomatic aims and the military operation’s course need to be assessed separately.
Securities regulation gains an institutional base
SEBI was constituted as a non-statutory body on 12 April 1988. It became a statutory body in 1992, with its Act taking effect from 30 January that year.

The regulator’s stated remit covers investor protection and securities-market development and regulation. Its administrative creation, statutory powers and subsequent enforcement record are separate parts of the history. The transition crosses the boundary between two eras.
Adult literacy becomes a national mission

The National Literacy Mission launched on 5 May 1988 to impart functional literacy to people aged 15–35 who were not literate. It added a focused adult-literacy effort to the education policy landscape.

Adult learning addressed people who had already missed formal schooling, rather than replacing expansion of school education. Campaign participation, reading and numeracy skills, and opportunities to retain those skills were different tests of progress.
The voting age falls from 21 to 18
The 61st Constitutional Amendment lowered the voting age for Lok Sabha and state assembly elections from 21 to 18. Parliament passed the amendment in 1988, and it took effect in March 1989.

The first general election had used a voting age of 21. The later reduction brought younger adults into the electorate. Eligibility to vote, registration and turnout are distinct stages of electoral participation.
A specific law against caste atrocities

The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in 1989 and came into force on 30 January 1990. It provided for specified offences, special courts and relief and rehabilitation.

This framework extended beyond the 1955 law against untouchability. Its existence recognised the need for specific protections. Assessing enforcement requires evidence on reporting, investigation, trials and support for victims.
Insurgency and forced displacement in Kashmir
As militancy escalated, targeted attacks and threats drove large numbers of Kashmiri Pandits from the Valley in 1990 and afterwards. Other communities also experienced displacement.

The loss of homes and security became a lasting crisis. The wider conflict involved insurgent violence and state security operations. Later administrative counts of registered migrant families do not measure a single day’s departures.
After the 1989 election, V. P. Singh formed a National Front government supported from outside by the BJP and Left parties.
Regional parties and negotiated parliamentary support became central to national government. Coalition politics had earlier precedents, including Janata.
Mandal brings representation to the centre
The V. P. Singh government announced implementation of the Mandal Commission's recommendation for OBC reservation in central government employment.
Support and opposition reshaped national politics around caste, representation and social justice. The policy's legal development continued through later court decisions.
The Ayodhya movement becomes a national mobilisation
BJP leader L. K. Advani began a Rath Yatra from Somnath on 25 September 1990 in support of the Ram temple movement at Ayodhya.

The mobilisation brought religious identity into national political competition alongside the debate over Mandal. This phase preceded the demolition of the Babri Masjid in December 1992, covered in the next era.
Another short premiership before the 1991 election
Chandra Shekhar became prime minister on 10 November 1990, succeeding V. P. Singh. His tenure continued until 21 June 1991.
The quick change of leadership forms part of the transition from single-party dominance to governments dependent on negotiated parliamentary backing.
Rajiv Gandhi is assassinated during the election campaign
Former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991 while campaigning in Tamil Nadu. The attack was linked to the LTTE.

His death changed Congress leadership during the election. Congress subsequently emerged as the largest party, and P. V. Narasimha Rao became prime minister. The next era follows the economic decisions of that government.
overview: Begin with the Emergency and the response to it. Restrictions on political freedom coexisted with legislation on bonded labour and equal remuneration. These laws need examination on their own terms, without treating them as a measure of democratic freedom. The 1977 election, the inquiry into abuses and constitutional safeguards were followed by Janata’s collapse and Congress’s return.

The 1980s combined expanded public responsibilities with major failures of protection. Child-development services, adult literacy, air and forest regulation, and consumer remedies addressed different needs. Satellite services and Rakesh Sharma’s flight marked distinct space achievements; Delhi hosted the Asian Games before the cricket World Cup victory. Punjab, the anti-Sikh killings and Bhopal exposed different forms of violence and vulnerability. Assam and Mizoram pursued distinct settlements, and statehood changed the federal map.

The closing years connect the Bofors allegations and accountability dispute with the 1989 election, followed by Mandal, the Ayodhya mobilisation and the displacement of Kashmiri Pandits. These were distinct developments with overlapping political consequences. SAARC and intervention in Sri Lanka also show contrasting regional commitments. The chapter ends with Rajiv Gandhi’s assassination during the 1991 election campaign. The next chapter takes up the economic crisis and reforms.

eras.title: Economic Liberalisation & Globalisation
eras.question: What changes when an economy opens up?
eras.intro: A foreign-exchange crisis brought urgent policy changes in 1991. Trade, investment and industrial rules changed over the following years, while telecom and software services found larger markets. Governments depended increasingly on alliances. Education programmes, local democracy and demands for representation developed alongside communal violence and national security crises.
eras.tension: Opening markets required rules, regulators and public investment. Faster growth in some industries did not mean equal opportunity across regions or occupations. Economic reform also unfolded alongside arguments over social representation, religious identity and the powers of the Union and states.
events: The rupee adjustment precedes a wider exchange-rate reform
The rupee was devalued in two steps on 1 and 3 July 1991. A dual exchange-rate system followed in March 1992, with the rates unified in March 1993.

Current-account convertibility followed in August 1994. This concerned payments such as trade and services, rather than unrestricted movement of all capital. The sequence extended beyond the July 1991 Budget.

On 24 July 1991, the Rao government announced a new industrial policy and Manmohan Singh presented the Union Budget amid a severe foreign-exchange crisis. Industrial licensing was reduced and trade, investment and financial-sector rules changed in stages.

Stabilising external payments and changing the economy’s longer-term rules were related tasks. Reform built on earlier changes and continued under later governments. Delicensing, disinvestment and global integration did not follow a single timetable or reach every sector equally.
A national programme organises the response to HIV/AIDS
The first National AIDS Control Programme launched in 1992, and the National AIDS Control Organisation was constituted to implement it. The first programme phase ran from 1992 to 1999.

Institutional coordination added a public-health dimension to the reform years. The programme’s creation should be distinguished from later changes in prevention, detection, treatment and access. Its launch did not by itself establish control of the epidemic.
The securities scandal exposes weaknesses in market oversight
Investigations in April 1992 uncovered serious irregularities in securities transactions involving banks and financial institutions. The RBI-appointed Janakiraman Committee examined the transactions.

The episode exposed weaknesses in transaction controls and supervision. It belongs alongside the history of market reform and SEBI’s statutory powers. SEBI’s earlier establishment in 1988 should not be attributed to the scandal.
The Mandal judgment upholds OBC reservation with conditions
On 16 November 1992, the Supreme Court’s Indra Sawhney judgment upheld 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in Union government civil posts and services, subject to exclusion of the creamy layer.

The judgment followed the 1990 implementation decision and its legal challenge. It shaped eligibility for reservation, while the identification of beneficiaries and administration of the policy required further action.
The Babri Masjid was demolished on 6 December 1992. Communal violence followed.
The event had lasting effects on politics, law and religious relations. Later legal decisions and the construction of the Ram temple belong to the continuing history, not to the 1992 event itself.

The 73rd and 74th Amendments were passed in 1992. The panchayat provisions came into force on 24 April 1993 and the municipal provisions on 1 June 1993, strengthening elected local government’s constitutional basis.

The framework covered regular elections and reservations, including for women. It did not create local government from nothing. State legislation and decisions about functions, funds and staff shaped how much authority local bodies exercised.
A series of bomb explosions struck Bombay, now Mumbai, on 12 March 1993, killing hundreds and injuring many more. Targets included public and commercial locations.
The attacks led to extensive investigations and criminal proceedings. Their history needs to distinguish the violence itself, the prosecution’s allegations and findings reached in individual cases.
A national commission takes up human-rights oversight

The National Human Rights Commission was established on 12 October 1993. Its functions include inquiries into human-rights violations or negligence in their prevention by public servants, review of safeguards and recommendations for action.

The Commission added a dedicated oversight institution alongside courts and other authorities. Its inquiry and recommendation functions should be distinguished from a court’s power to convict. Institutional creation alone does not establish effective redress for every complainant.
Telecom policy opens space for private investment

The National Telecom Policy of 1994 sought private investment alongside the Department of Telecommunications. The 1999 policy revisited the framework after slower-than-expected private entry and financial difficulties for operators.

Later mobile and internet growth followed policy changes across several governments. The 1999 document itself acknowledged that some earlier targets remained unmet. A policy target is not evidence of a completed rollout.
Judicial review limits the use of President’s Rule
In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India, decided on 11 March 1994, the Supreme Court held that proclamations under Article 356 were subject to judicial review.

The judgment became a major reference point for the protection of federalism and state governments. It did not abolish President’s Rule. The legal justification for a proclamation and a political disagreement with a state government are different questions.
PSLV successfully places IRS-P2 in orbit
PSLV-D2 successfully launched the IRS-P2 remote-sensing satellite on 15 October 1994. ISRO records this second developmental flight as a successful milestone in the launch vehicle programme.

Domestic launch capability developed through testing and successive missions. This success was distinct from the programme’s earlier developmental attempt and from later commercial or exploration missions. It adds space engineering to the era’s account of technological change.
Electronic equity trading changes market infrastructure
The National Stock Exchange began trading in its equities segment on 3 November 1994. Its electronic trading system formed part of the changes in market infrastructure during the reform years.

The story of market reform includes the systems through which orders are matched and transactions recorded. A new trading platform did not remove investment risk or the need for supervision, a distinction made sharper by the securities scandal earlier in the decade.
India joins the World Trade Organization
India became a WTO member on 1 January 1995. Its participation in the earlier GATT system dated to 8 July 1948.

The milestone placed India within the new multilateral trade organisation. It was not India’s first engagement with international trade rules. Membership, domestic economic reform and the distribution of trade’s benefits are related but distinct subjects.
Pulse Polio begins nationwide immunisation rounds
The nationwide Pulse Polio immunisation programme launched in 1995. National Immunisation Days became part of the campaign against polio.

Repeated vaccination rounds, surveillance and reaching missed children were different parts of the effort. The campaign’s start should not be confused with the later interruption of wild-poliovirus transmission or the WHO regional certification recorded in the next chapter.
Public internet services launched in India on 15 August 1995. The launch preceded the later spread of private internet providers, broadband and mobile data.

This was a public-service milestone, not the first use of computer networks in India. Access at launch should not be confused with widespread household connectivity. The transition to mass use took many more years.
A national school-nutrition programme links food and attendance

The National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education launched on 15 August 1995, initially in 2,408 blocks. A Supreme Court order of 28 November 2001 subsequently directed provision of cooked midday meals under the scheme.
